props.title: Communion

sections.content: Communion (1989) represents a fascinating intersection of alien abduction cinema and psychological horror, with Christopher Walken delivering an unforgettably eccentric performance as Whitley Strieber, the real-life author whose claimed encounters with "visitors" sparked widespread debate. The film follows similar thematic territory as Fire in the Sky (1993) but takes a more cerebral, ambiguous approach. Unlike the visceral horror of The Fourth Kind (2009), Communion delves deeper into the psychological implications of its protagonist's experiences, leaving viewers to question whether they're witnessing actual extraterrestrial contact or a mind unraveling.

sections.content: What sets Communion apart from contemporary alien films like Alien 3 (1992) or Body Snatchers (1993) is its deeply personal nature. Director Philippe Mora approaches the material with an art house sensibility, creating dreamlike sequences that blur the line between reality and hallucination. The film's infamous "blue room" sequences, where Walken encounters the "visitors," employ practical effects and surreal imagery that feel more reminiscent of David Lynch's Eraserhead (1977) than traditional sci-fi horror.

The film's impact on alien abduction culture cannot be understated. Along with The UFO Incident (1975) about the Betty and Barney Hill case, Communion helped establish many of the visual tropes we associate with alien encounters - particularly the "grey" aliens with their large black eyes. The film's approach to memory recovery through hypnosis influenced later works like Dark Skies (2013) and elements of The X-Files (1993-2018). SUBHEAD: Psychological Horror and Reality

sections.content: Communion shares DNA with psychological horror films like Jacob's Ladder (1990) and In the Mouth of Madness (1994), where reality itself becomes suspect. Walken's portrayal of Strieber captures the author's real-life ambivalence about his experiences - he never definitively claims alien abduction, instead using the term "visitors" and remaining open to multiple interpretations. This complexity elevates the film above simple belief-versus-skepticism narratives common in alien encounter movies like Signs (2002).
